blocks.text: Long ago, the good god Osiris was king of Egypt, and his wife Isis was queen. Osiris taught the people of Egypt how to grow crops, and gave them good laws, and taught them to honour the gods. Then he travelled all over the world, teaching other people too. He never made them obey him by fighting. Instead, he won them over with kind words, and with songs and music.
While Osiris was away, Queen Isis ruled Egypt, and she ruled it well.

But Osiris had a wicked brother, called Set. When Osiris came home, Set made a cunning plan against him. He got seventy-two people to help him. Then he secretly measured Osiris's body, and had a chest made exactly the same size. It was a beautiful chest, decorated all over.
Set brought the chest to a great feast, and everyone admired it. "I'll give this chest," said Set, as if it were a joke, "to whoever fits inside it exactly!"
So, one after another, all the guests lay down in the chest. But it did not fit any of them. Last of all, Osiris lay down in it. And it fitted him perfectly.

At once Set and his helpers ran up and slammed the lid down, and nailed it shut, and sealed it with melted lead. Then they carried the chest to the river Nile, and threw it in. And the river carried it away, down to the sea.

When Isis heard what had happened, she cut off a lock of her hair and put on mourning clothes. Then she wandered all over the country, looking for the chest, and asking everyone she met if they had seen it. At last some children told her which way the river had carried it.

The waves had carried the chest across the sea, to the shore of a land called Byblos. There it came to rest in a little tamarisk bush. The bush grew and grew into a great, beautiful tree, and its trunk grew all the way round the chest, so that the chest was hidden inside it.
The king of Byblos admired the great tree. He had it cut down, and used the part of the trunk with the chest inside it as a pillar to hold up the roof of his palace.

Isis found out where the chest was, and went to Byblos. She sat down by a fountain, and spoke to no one except the queen's maids. She was kind to them, and braided their hair, and a wonderful sweet smell came from her into their hair. When the queen smelled it, she wanted to meet the stranger. She invited Isis to the palace, and made her nurse to her baby son.

Every night, Isis put the baby in the fire, to burn away the part of him that would die, so that he would live for ever. And she turned herself into a swallow, and flew round and round the pillar, singing sadly. But one night the queen saw her baby in the flames, and screamed. And so the baby lost the chance to live for ever.

Then Isis showed the king and queen that she was a goddess, and asked for the pillar that held up their roof. They gave it to her. She cut it open, took out the chest, and gave the wood back to them, wrapped in fine linen and perfumed with oil. Then she threw herself on the chest and wept. And she sailed back to Egypt with it.
When she got home, Isis hid the chest in a lonely place, while she went to see her son Horus, who was being brought up in the town of Buto.

But one night Set went hunting by the light of the moon, and he came across the chest. He knew at once whose body was inside. In his rage, he tore the body into fourteen pieces, and scattered them all over Egypt.

When Isis found out, she set out again to look for her husband. She sailed all through the marshes in a boat made of papyrus reeds. And wherever she found a piece of Osiris, she made a tomb for it. That is why there are tombs of Osiris in many places in Egypt.
Then Osiris came back from the world of the dead, to visit his son Horus. He taught Horus how to fight, to get ready for the battle with Set.
"What is the most glorious thing a man can do?" Osiris asked him.
"To stand up for his father and mother, when someone has done them wrong," said Horus.
"And which animal is most useful in a battle?" asked Osiris.
"A horse," said Horus.
Osiris was surprised. "Why a horse," he asked, "and not a lion?"
"A lion is useful to someone who needs help," said Horus, "but a horse is better for chasing an enemy who runs away."
Then Osiris was very happy, because he knew his son was ready.

Horus fought a great battle against Set, which went on for many days. At last Horus won, and Set was taken prisoner. Horus gave Set to his mother Isis to guard. But Isis did not punish her brother. She untied him and let him go free.
Horus was so angry that he pulled the crown off his mother's head. But Thoth came, and gave Isis a new crown, shaped like the head of a cow.
Then Set told the gods that Horus was not really the son of Osiris, and had no right to be king. But with Thoth's help, the gods declared that Horus truly was his father's son.
Horus and Set fought two more battles, and Horus won both of them. And so Horus, the son of Osiris and Isis, became the rightful king of Egypt.

A simplified retelling of E. A. Wallis Budge's “The History of Isis and Osiris” in Legends of the Gods (1912). The original is listed under Other versions only when “Show stories with mature themes” is on in Settings. Plutarch calls Set by the Greek name Typhon, and Thoth by the name Hermes.
